title: Reverse Pairs
description: Count pairs (i, j) with i < j and nums[i] > 2*nums[j], using a modified merge sort that counts cross-half pairs during the merge.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given an integer array nums, return the number of "reverse pairs": pairs of indices (i, j) with i < j and nums[i] > 2 * nums[j].

blocks.caption: A modified merge sort counts cross-half reverse pairs during the merge step itself.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","nums[] (can contain negatives)"],["Reverse pair condition","i < j AND nums[i] > 2 * nums[j]"],["Output","Total count of such pairs across the whole array"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

Counting pairs with an order-and-comparison condition (i < j and a value relationship) across the WHOLE array is a classic modified-merge-sort problem: recursively split, and while both halves are still separately sorted (right before merging), count cross-half qualifying pairs in linear time using two pointers.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: This is the same divide-and-conquer counting technique as the classic "count inversions" problem, generalized from nums[i] > nums[j] to nums[i] > 2 * nums[j].
3. Understand the Problem

Picture recursively splitting the array in half, sorting each half, and merging them back together, just like standard merge sort. Right before merging two already-sorted halves, a two-pointer sweep can count, for every element in the left half, how many elements in the right half satisfy the reverse-pair condition, all in a single linear pass, since both halves are sorted.

blocks.caption: Both halves already sorted means the qualifying count sweep never needs to backtrack.

items: Recursively split the array in half, sorting each half via merge sort.
Before merging, use two pointers: for each left-half value (in order), advance a right-half pointer past every value satisfying left > 2*right, and add that count.
Merge the two halves normally, then return the accumulated count up the recursion, summing counts from every level.

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
nums = [1,3,2,3,1]. The recursion splits into [1,3] and [2,3,1], each sorted and merged bottom-up.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Merge step","Left, Right (already sorted)","Cross-half pairs counted"],"rows":[["1","[1] and [3]","1 > 2*3=6? no. 0 pairs"],["2","[3] and [1]","3 > 2*1=2? yes. 1 pair"],["3","[2] and [1,3]","2 > 2*1=2? no (not strictly greater). 0 pairs"],["4 (top level)","[1,3] and [1,2,3]","3 > 2*1=2, yes, 1 pair; no other qualifying pair"]]}

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: Summing counts across all merge steps (0+1+0+1) gives 2 total reverse pairs, matching the expected output.
5. How Should We Think?
A direct approach checks every pair (i, j) with i < j directly, which is correct but quadratic.

Merge sort naturally divides the problem into halves and re-sorts them; the key insight is that the counting step can be inserted right before merging, since both halves are independently sorted at that point, letting a two-pointer sweep count all cross-half qualifying pairs in linear time rather than checking every pair individually.
6. Brute Force Solution
Check every pair (i, j) with i < j directly for the reverse-pair condition.
7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n^2)","Every pair is checked directly"],["Space","O(1)","No extra storage beyond the counter"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: For large n, checking every pair individually is far more work than necessary once merge sort's divide-and-conquer structure can count cross-half pairs in bulk.
8. Optimize the Solution

Perform merge sort, but right before merging two sorted halves, count cross-half reverse pairs with a two-pointer sweep: for each left-half element (already in sorted order), advance the right-half pointer past every element satisfying the reverse-pair condition, adding that count. Since the right pointer only ever moves forward across the whole sweep, this counting step is linear.

items: Recursively sort both halves via merge sort.
Before merging, two-pointer sweep counts cross-half reverse pairs in O(left.length + right.length).
Merge normally, then return the count, accumulated across every recursive call.

blocks.text: 9. Optimized Solution

codes.python:
def reverse_pairs(nums):
    count = 0

    def merge_sort(arr):
        nonlocal count
        if len(arr) <= 1:
            return arr

        mid = len(arr) // 2
        left = merge_sort(arr[:mid])
        right = merge_sort(arr[mid:])

        j = 0
        for i in range(len(left)):
            while j < len(right) and left[i] > 2 * right[j]:
                j += 1
            count += j

        merged = []
        li = ri = 0
        while li < len(left) and ri < len(right):
            if left[li] <= right[ri]:
                merged.append(left[li])
                li += 1
            else:
                merged.append(right[ri])
                ri += 1
        merged.extend(left[li:])
        merged.extend(right[ri:])
        return merged

    merge_sort(nums)
    return count


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(reverse_pairs([1, 3, 2, 3, 1]))
    print(reverse_pairs([2, 4, 3, 5, 1]))

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space"],"rows":[["Brute Force, all-pairs check","O(n^2)","O(1)"],["Optimized, modified merge sort","O(n log n)","O(n)"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Counting cross-index pairs with an ordering condition across a whole array is a classic modified-merge-sort technique.
The counting step must happen BEFORE merging, while both halves are still separately (not jointly) sorted, since that is what makes the two-pointer sweep linear.
This generalizes the classic "count inversions" pattern to any comparison condition between elements, not just simple greater-than.

blocks.text: 12. Final Summary

Reverse Pairs is solved with a modified merge sort: right before merging two already-sorted halves, a two-pointer sweep counts cross-half reverse pairs in linear time, since both halves are sorted at that point. Summing this count across every level of the recursion gives the total in O(n log n) time.
